Price Increase for GPU Servers
 - cloudscale.ch
highlights:
## Price Increase for GPU Servers 

AI is currently the number one topic. Here at cloudscale, we have also seen a sharp increase in demand for our GPU servers over the past few months. We are currently procuring additional hardware so that you can keep using GPU resources whenever you need them in the future. However, due to the current situation on the hardware markets, a price increase is unavoidable; the new prices will apply to GPU servers created or scaled on or after 2026-09-01.

...

In early 2026, we switched to NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q GPUs, which offer you even more performance and twice the amount of VRAM.

This offering has proven to be highly popular and has been completely booked out at both cloud locations during certain periods over the past few weeks. We are therefore in the process of procuring additional hardware so that we can once again provide you with the GPU servers you need at any time – even instantly. For you, nothing will change in terms of specs: We are still convinced of the performance of the RTX PRO 6000 Max-Q, and the feedback from our customers confirms this. We expect to have the additional hardware up and running by the end of August or early September – although, given the current procurement situation, nothing can be guaranteed.

### Necessary price adjustment

Speaking of the hardware market: You may have noticed the recent price trends – within just a few months, GPU prices have doubled, SSD prices have increased fivefold, and RAM module prices have even risen tenfold or more! Since we deliberately rely on open-source software, we also avoid vendor lock-in when it comes to hardware – that is, being restricted to just a few components certified as "compatible". However, with purchase prices rising across the board, we too had to recalculate our prices when procuring the additional GPU hosts. (Let us know if you would like to learn more about the hardware at cloudscale; if there is enough interest, we will dedicate a separate post to the topic.)

Of course, we are trying to limit the price increase to the necessary minimum. Therefore, only the price of our "GPU2" flavors will change, and only for GPU servers that are newly created or scaled starting 2026-09-01. In this context, "scaling" means changing the GPU flavor; specifically:

- more or less memory than before
- more or fewer CPU cores than before
- more or fewer GPUs than before
- increasing the scratch disk size (reducing it is not possible)

Changes to other features of GPU servers do not trigger a price adjustment for the GPU server. For example:

- increasing the size of the root volume
- attaching or increasing the size of additional NVMe SSD and Bulk volumes
- adding or removing Floating IPs
- attaching or removing private networks

In these cases, you only pay for the additional space or IP address – the price of the GPU server itself remains unchanged.

You can already find the new prices on our website. However, until 2026-08-31, you will still benefit from the old price displayed in the cloud control panel.

If you already have a GPU server or – subject to availability – create one by 2026-08-31, you will continue to pay the current price for that server until further notice. All "Flex" and "Plus" flavors, as well as other features, will also remain unaffected by the price increase for the time being.

results.title: Hugging Face vs Fireworks AI: Router or Direct API in 2026 | Markaicode
highlights:
Two things surfaced during this revision that are worth flagging explicitly: first, Llama 3.1 8B and 70B Instruct — the models most third-party pricing trackers, and an earlier draft of this article, use as the illustrative example for Fireworks' size-based pricing tiers — no longer support Fireworks' serverless endpoint as of this writing. Fireworks' own model pages for both now list "Serverless: Not supported," leaving them available only for on-demand deployment or fine-tuning. This revision uses currently-serverless models instead. Second, Fireworks raised its on-demand GPU rate from $7.00/hr to $8.00/hr on September 1, 2026; every on-demand dollar figure below reflects the post-increase rate.

...

| Dimension | Hugging Face (Inference Providers) | Fireworks AI (direct) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it actually is | A router in front of roughly 17 third-party inference platforms (as of September 2026), plus its own first-party `hf-inference` compute | A single inference platform that runs its own GPU fleet |
| Model access | Whatever its partner providers expose — includes Fireworks' own catalog when you pin the `fireworks-ai` provider | Fireworks' own curated catalog (100+ open-weight and closed-weight models per its model library) |
| Billing | One Hugging Face bill; routed requests billed at the underlying provider's rate, no markup | Prepaid credits; your spend tier (Tier 1–4, reached by adding $0–$5,000+ in credits) sets your rate-limit ceiling |
| Free tier | $0.10/month Inference Provider credit (Free), pooled $2/seat/month (PRO or Enterprise) | $1 one-time signup credit — no ongoing monthly free tier |
| Entry subscription | PRO $9/month (higher rate limits, ZeroGPU compute, more storage); Team $20/user/month | None required; pay-as-you-go once a valid card is on file |
| Serverless pricing — generic 4B–16B tier | Same as the underlying provider's rate when routed | $0.20 per 1M tokens |
| Serverless pricing — generic >16B tier | Same pass-through logic | $0.90 per 1M tokens |
| Serverless pricing — named flagship model (e.g., GLM 5.3) | Same pass-through logic | Priced individually, not by the generic tier — GLM 5.3 Standard: $1.40 input / $4.40 output per 1M tokens |
| Dedicated GPU option | Inference Endpoints, by GPU and cloud: T4 $0.50/hr, L4 $0.70–0.80/hr, A10G $1.00/hr, A100 $2.50/hr (AWS) or $3.60/hr (GCP), H100 $4.50/hr (AWS) or $10/hr (GCP), H200 $5/hr, B200 $9.25/hr | On-demand: H100 or H200 $8.00/hr, B200 $13.00/hr, B300 $15.00/hr (rates effective September 1, 2026) |
| Fine-tuning | Not a first-party feature of Inference Providers itself | LoRA supervised fine-tuning from $0.50 per 1M training tokens (models up to 16B parameters) |
| Compliance | Hub, Inference Endpoints, and Inference Providers are SOC 2 Type II certified; GDPR data processing agreements and HIPAA BAAs available on Enterprise | SOC 2 Type II and HIPAA compliant; ISO 27001, 27701, and 42001 certified; zero data retention on open models unless you opt in |
| Vendor lock-in | Lower — swap providers behind one API without changing client code | Higher — you're on Fireworks' catalog and terms |

...

Fireworks prices most of its long-tail catalog by model-size tier: sub-4B models at $0.10 per 1M tokens, 4B–16B models at $0.20 per 1M, and models above 16B parameters at $0.90 per 1M, per Fireworks' own serverless pricing page. Named flagship models — GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, DeepSeek V4, and similar — are priced individually instead of by the generic tier, and those individual rates are usually higher than the generic $0.90 ceiling; check the specific model's row before assuming the tier price applies. There's no ongoing free serverless tier, only a $1 signup credit. Fireworks runs on prepaid credits: adding credits raises your spend tier, which in turn raises your account-wide rate-limit ceiling (10 RPM with no payment method, up to a fixed 6,000 RPM cap once you're funded). Fireworks also rents dedicated GPUs by the hour (H100 or H200 at $8.00/hr as of September 1, 2026) and offers LoRA supervised fine-tuning from $0.50 per 1M training tokens for models up to 16B parameters — a feature Hugging Face's router doesn't provide itself.

...

If cost is the deciding factor between Fireworks' serverless per-token billing (either path — the price is identical) and its on-demand dedicated GPU, here's the crossover math, current as of September 2026. A single on-demand H100 or H200 costs $8.00/hr; run continuously that's $8 × 730 hours/month ≈ $5,840/month. Fireworks' generic serverless rate for open-weight models above 16B parameters is $0.90 per 1M tokens. Dividing, $5,840 ÷ $0.90 × 1,000,000 ≈ 6.5 billion tokens/month is the rough crossover — below that sustained volume, serverless is cheaper; above it, a dedicated GPU starts winning, assuming full utilization and no idle time. This assumes continuous (730 hr/month) usage and the generic >16B tier rate; a named flagship model with its own higher per-token rate (like GLM 5.3) will cross over at a lower token volume, so re-run this division with the specific model's actual rate before committing.

results.title: H100 Rental Prices by Region, Q3 2026: Premium Halved
highlights:
At the start of 2025, renting an H100 from a hyperscaler cost 3 to 4.5 times the non-hyperscaler rate, depending on region. As of Q3 2026, the multiple averages roughly 2 to 2.5 times. The premium is still substantial, at about 120% on average across the seven regions we track, but it is close to half what it was eighteen months ago.

...

Hyperscalers price H100 rentals at a persistent premium to non-hyperscaler providers, the tier often described as neoclouds, in every region we track. The premium reflects more than the GPU. Hyperscaler rates bundle ancillary value that non-hyperscaler providers typically do not carry: managed orchestration and the surrounding platform services, enterprise support agreements and SLAs, certified compliance regimes for regulated workloads, security posture that has already cleared enterprise procurement review, and integration with the data, storage, and networking ecosystem a large customer is often already running on. Buyers paying the premium are, at least in part, paying for that bundle, and for some workloads, regulated inference close to existing cloud data being the clearest case, the bundle is the product.

...

The narrowing since Q1 2025 is primarily a hyperscaler story. Hyperscaler H100 rates fell in every region, but at very different speeds: roughly 26% in US East, around 30% in US West and the Middle East, just over 40% in Canada, the Nordics, and Europe, and about 54% in Asia-Pacific, the steepest decline in the panel.

Most of that adjustment happened in two steps. The first was a sharp reset around Q3 2025, visible as a cliff in nearly every regional chart, after which several regions sat flat for two or more consecutive quarters. The second was a slower grind through the first half of 2026. The timing of the first step coincides with the period in which B200 capacity began arriving at scale, consistent with newer-generation supply repricing the H100 tier below it, though the quarterly series alone cannot attribute the move to any single cause.

Non-hyperscaler rates tell a different story. They dipped through mid-2025, US East touched roughly $1.35 in Q3 2025 and Canada and the Nordics bottomed near $1.60 to $1.75 in early 2026, before recovering into 2026. By Q3 2026, non-hyperscaler rates in US East and the Nordics sit at or above their Q1 2025 levels, around $2.90 and $3.30 respectively. A falling numerator and a recovering denominator compressed the ratio from both sides.

...

As of the partial third quarter of 2026, quarterly median rental prices per hour in the regions we track run roughly $2.00 to $3.30 at non-hyperscaler (neocloud) providers and roughly $4.80 to $6.10 at hyperscalers, depending on region.
- Which region has the cheapest H100 rentals?

...

- What is the difference between a hyperscaler and a neocloud?

Hyperscalers are the large integrated cloud platforms that sell GPU compute as part of a broad managed ecosystem of software, compliance, and platform services. Neoclouds are specialized GPU cloud providers that sell capacity closer to the bare GPU-hour, typically at lower rates with a thinner service layer. The price gap between the two tiers is the premium this article measures.

### Neocloud providers

Neocloud providers are GPU-focused clouds optimized for high-intensity AI training, offering the latest NVIDIA chips and fast interconnects that support distributed training at scale. Unlike general-purpose clouds, they exist primarily to maximize performance for compute-heavy workloads, often with premium pricing to match.

#### 12. CoreWeave for teams training frontier-scale models

CoreWeave provides configurable GPU instances for users with specific, resource-heavy workloads, such as machine learning, rendering, VFX, and simulations. As a neocloud provider, CoreWeave focuses on delivering high-performance computing at scale, offering access to NVIDIA GPUs, high-bandwidth networking, and specialized infrastructure for distributed training.

CoreWeave’s platform is built around speed and scale, with fast provisioning and performance-optimized clusters tailored to AI workloads. However, users should be aware of potential downsides, including additional networking or storage fees that can make total cost less predictable. CoreWeave also lacks some of the simplified onboarding resources (like starter templates or pre-built images) seen in more general-purpose clouds, and its pricing is typically higher than traditional providers.

CoreWeave key features:

- Fast provisioning and autoscaling designed for teams running demanding, bursty workloads.
- Specialized clusters tailored for ML training, rendering, and VFX pipelines.
- Optimized performance for large-scale compute, including support for high-throughput workloads and advanced interconnects.

CoreWeave GPU options and pricing:

- CoreWeave supports GPUs like the NVIDIA A100, H100, H200, L40S, plus the AMD Genoa and Turin. Pricing ranges from $5.31 to $68.80 per hour, based on the resources requested or consumed within each minute.

#### 13. Lambda Labs for ML researchers requiring high-end training GPUs

Lambda Labs has centered AI as its focus since its initial founding, building deep learning servers and workstations before moving into the cloud GPU space more recently. It’s particularly known for both its developer-friendly platform and competitive pricing. Its Lambda Stack offers a curated set of software packages—including TensorFlow, PyTorch, and Ubuntu—confirmed compatible across their systems and GPUs.

One consideration with Lambda Labs is that capacity can be limited for certain GPU types, especially during periods of high demand. Some GPUs or clusters may only be available in specific regions.

results.title: Modal Pricing 2026: The Real Serverless GPU Bill
highlights:
Modal (modal.com) has three plans in 2026: Starter at $0 a month with $30 of free compute credit, Team at $250 a month with $100 of free credit, and custom Enterprise. Compute on top is metered per second with scale-to-zero. GPU rates work out to about $3.95 an hour for an H100, $2.50 for an A100 80GB, $1.95 for an L40S, $1.10 for an A10, and $0.80 for an L4. CPU is $0.047 per physical core-hour, memory is $0.008 per GiB-hour, and storage volumes are $0.09 per GiB a month with the first 1 TiB free. Network egress is $0.04 per GiB above a monthly plan allowance of 1 TiB on Starter, 10 TiB on Team and 100 TiB on Enterprise, and Modal began charging it on October 1, 2026. For most workloads the invoice is still almost entirely GPU-seconds, and the number that decides it is how long your containers stay warm, not how many requests you serve.
